questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: A function \( f \) is continuous at \( x=a \) if and only if which condition holds?
options: \( \lim_{x\to a^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^{+}}f(x) \) only, regardless of \( f(a) \)
\( f(a) \) exists, regardless of the limit
questions.explanation:
Continuity at a point requires three quantities to all agree.

The left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and the function's value at that point must all be equal: \( \lim_{x\to a^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^{+}}f(x)=f(a) \).
questions.hint: Continuity needs three quantities, not just two, to match.
distractor_logic: Matching one-sided limits without checking against \( f(a) \) only confirms the limit exists, not that it equals the function value
Existence of \( f(a) \) alone says nothing about whether the limit exists or matches it
This describes a discontinuity (LHL not equal to RHL), the opposite of continuity

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Which class of functions is continuous at every real number?
options: Every rational function, including at points where the denominator is zero
Only linear functions of the form \( f(x)=mx+c \)
No algebraic function is continuous everywhere
questions.explanation:
A polynomial is built only from sums and products of \( x \) with constants.

Since sums and products of continuous functions are continuous, every polynomial function is continuous at every real number.
questions.hint: Think about what operations build up a polynomial.
distractor_logic: Rational functions fail to be continuous exactly where the denominator vanishes, so they are not continuous everywhere
Linear functions are just one special case of the larger, correct class
Polynomials are a standard example of functions that are continuous everywhere

questions.question: If \( f \) and \( g \) are both continuous at \( x=a \), what is true of \( f+g \) and \( f-g \) at \( x=a \)?
options: Only \( f+g \) is continuous at \( x=a \), not \( f-g \)
Neither is guaranteed to be continuous at \( x=a \)
Both \( f+g \) and \( f-g \) are continuous at \( x=a \)
They are continuous only if \( f(a)=g(a) \)
questions.explanation:
The algebra of continuous functions guarantees closure under addition and subtraction.

If \( f \) and \( g \) are continuous at \( x=a \), then \( f+g \) and \( f-g \) are also continuous at \( x=a \), with no extra condition required.
questions.hint: Sum and difference of continuous functions behave the same way.
distractor_logic: Difference behaves identically to sum under this rule; there is no such asymmetry
This wrongly denies that continuity of sums and differences is guaranteed at all
No such condition relating \( f(a) \) and \( g(a) \) is required

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: If \( f \) and \( g \) are both continuous at \( x=a \), what is guaranteed about \( f(x)\cdot g(x) \) at \( x=a \)?
options: \( f\cdot g \) is continuous at \( x=a \) only if \( f(a)\neq0 \) and \( g(a)\neq0 \)
\( f\cdot g \) is continuous at \( x=a \) only if \( f=g \)
Nothing can be concluded about \( f\cdot g \) without more information
\( f\cdot g \) is continuous at \( x=a \), with no extra condition
questions.explanation:
The algebra of continuous functions includes closure under multiplication.

If \( f \) and \( g \) are continuous at \( x=a \), the product \( f\cdot g \) is automatically continuous at \( x=a \), with no restriction on the values \( f(a) \) or \( g(a) \).
questions.hint: The product rule for continuity has no extra hypothesis, unlike the quotient rule.
distractor_logic: This wrongly imports the nonzero-denominator condition from the quotient rule into the product rule
There is no requirement that \( f \) and \( g \) be equal
The conclusion actually follows directly from \( f \) and \( g \) individually being continuous

questions.question: If \( f \) and \( g \) are both continuous at \( x=a \), under what condition is \( \dfrac{f}{g} \) continuous at \( x=a \)?
questions.explanation:
Division introduces one extra requirement beyond continuity of \( f \) and \( g \) themselves.

The quotient \( \dfrac{f}{g} \) is continuous at \( x=a \) provided \( g(a)\neq0 \), since division by zero is undefined there.
questions.hint: Only the denominator being zero can break this one.
distractor_logic: It is the denominator \( g(a) \), not the numerator \( f(a) \), whose non-vanishing matters here
Ignoring the nonzero-denominator condition entirely is incorrect, since division by zero must be excluded
No such equality condition between \( f(a) \) and \( g(a) \) is needed

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: What is the standard notation for the left-hand limit of \( f \) as \( x \) approaches \( a \)?
questions.explanation:
The left-hand limit records the behaviour of \( f \) as \( x \) approaches \( a \) from values smaller than \( a \).

This is written with a superscript minus sign directly on \( a \): \( \lim_{x\to a^{-}}f(x) \).
questions.hint: The minus sign sits as a superscript on \( a \) itself, showing the direction of approach.
distractor_logic: This superscript plus sign denotes the right-hand limit instead, the opposite direction
Placing the minus sign on \( a \) itself changes the target point to \( -a \), not the direction of approach
Negating the argument of \( f \) is a different operation from specifying the direction of approach

questions.question: What is the standard notation for the right-hand limit of \( f \) as \( x \) approaches \( a \)?
questions.explanation:
The right-hand limit records the behaviour of \( f \) as \( x \) approaches \( a \) from values larger than \( a \).

This is written with a superscript plus sign directly on \( a \): \( \lim_{x\to a^{+}}f(x) \).
questions.hint: The plus sign sits as a superscript on \( a \) itself.
distractor_logic: This superscript minus sign denotes the left-hand limit instead, the opposite direction
Placing the plus sign on \( a \) itself changes nothing meaningful, since \( +a \) is just \( a \), and loses the direction information

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: A rational function \( f(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} \), with \( p \) and \( q \) polynomials, is continuous at every point where:
options: It is continuous everywhere, with no exceptions
questions.explanation:
A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials, and polynomials are continuous everywhere.

By the quotient rule for continuous functions, \( \dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)} \) is continuous at every \( x \) in its domain, i.e. wherever \( q(x)\neq0 \).
questions.hint: Only the denominator's zeros can cause trouble.
distractor_logic: It is the denominator \( q(x) \), not the numerator \( p(x) \), whose vanishing matters for continuity here
There is no requirement that the numerator equal the denominator
Rational functions are undefined, and hence not continuous, at the zeros of the denominator, so this overstates the claim

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: A function is defined as \( f(x)=\begin{cases}3x+1,& x\leq2\\ 4x-1,& x>2\end{cases} \). Check the continuity of \( f \) at \( x=2 \).
options: Discontinuous at \( x=2 \), since \( f(2) \) is undefined
Continuous at \( x=2 \), but only because \( f(2)=6 \)
questions.explanation:
Compute the left-hand limit using the first piece: \( \lim_{x\to2^{-}}(3x+1)=3(2)+1=7 \).

Compute the right-hand limit using the second piece: \( \lim_{x\to2^{+}}(4x-1)=4(2)-1=7 \).

Since \( x=2 \) falls in the first piece, \( f(2)=3(2)+1=7 \).

All three values equal \( 7 \), so \( f \) is continuous at \( x=2 \).
questions.hint: Compute LHL, RHL, and \( f(2) \) separately using the correct piece for each.
distractor_logic: This reports an arithmetic slip, \( 4(2)-1=6 \) instead of the correct \( 7 \), which wrongly suggests the one-sided limits disagree
\( f(2) \) is defined by the first piece since its condition is \( x\leq2 \), so it does exist and equals \( 7 \)
This uses the same slipped value \( 6 \) for \( f(2) \) instead of the correct \( 7 \), so the reasoning given does not actually match the true computation

questions.question: A function is defined as \( f(x)=\begin{cases}x^{2}-1,& x<3\\ 2x+2,& x\geq3\end{cases} \). Check the continuity of \( f \) at \( x=3 \).
options: Discontinuous at \( x=3 \), since \( \lim_{x\to3^{-}}f(x)=9 \) but \( f(3)=8 \)
Discontinuous at \( x=3 \), since \( \lim_{x\to3^{+}}f(x) \) does not exist
Cannot be determined, since the two pieces use different formulas
questions.explanation:
Compute the left-hand limit using the first piece: \( \lim_{x\to3^{-}}(x^{2}-1)=3^{2}-1=8 \).

Compute the right-hand limit using the second piece: \( \lim_{x\to3^{+}}(2x+2)=2(3)+2=8 \).

Since \( x=3 \) falls in the second piece, \( f(3)=2(3)+2=8 \).

All three values equal \( 8 \), so \( f \) is continuous at \( x=3 \).
questions.hint: Compute all three quantities carefully using the correct piece for each.
distractor_logic: This reports an arithmetic slip, \( 3^2-1=9 \) instead of the correct \( 8 \), which wrongly suggests a mismatch
The right-hand limit does exist and is finite, since the second piece \( 2x+2 \) is a polynomial
Using different formulas on the two sides is completely normal for a piecewise function; continuity is decided by comparing LHL, RHL and \( f(3) \), which can all be computed directly

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2},& x\neq2\\ k,& x=2\end{cases} \). Find the value of \( k \) that makes \( f \) continuous at \( x=2 \).
options: No value of \( k \) works, since the limit does not exist
questions.explanation:
For \( x\neq2 \), factor: \( \dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}=\dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2 \).

So \( \lim_{x\to2}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2}(x+2)=4 \).

For continuity at \( x=2 \), \( f(2)=k \) must equal this limit, so \( k=4 \).
questions.hint: Factor and cancel first; direct substitution gives \( 0/0 \).
distractor_logic: This is the value of \( x \) at the join point itself, mistaken for the required limit value
This would arise from wrongly substituting \( x=2 \) directly into the unfactored expression and treating the resulting \( 0/0 \) form as equal to \( 0 \)
The limit does exist once the removable factor is cancelled; only a direct (invalid) substitution into \( 0/0 \) makes it look like it fails

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sin3x}{x},& x\neq0\\ k,& x=0\end{cases} \). Find the value of \( k \) that makes \( f \) continuous at \( x=0 \).
options: \( k \) cannot be found, since \( f \) has no limit at \( x=0 \)
questions.explanation:
Write \( \dfrac{\sin3x}{x}=3\cdot\dfrac{\sin3x}{3x} \).

As \( x\to0 \), \( 3x\to0 \) too, so \( \lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\sin3x}{3x}=1 \) by the standard trigonometric limit.

Hence \( \lim_{x\to0}f(x)=3\cdot1=3 \).

For continuity, \( k=f(0) \) must equal this limit, so \( k=3 \).
questions.hint: Rewrite so the argument of \( \sin \) matches the denominator exactly, then use \( \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1 \).
distractor_logic: This applies the standard limit \( \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1 \) directly without adjusting for the factor of \( 3 \) inside \( \sin3x \)
This treats the \( \frac{0}{0} \) form at \( x=0 \) as evaluating to \( 0 \) by naive direct substitution, instead of using the standard trigonometric limit
The limit does exist and is finite by the standard trigonometric limit; the function only appears problematic under naive direct substitution

questions.question: Let \( f(x)=x^{2} \) and \( g(x)=|x| \). Both are continuous at \( x=0 \). Is \( h(x)=f(x)\cdot g(x)=x^{2}|x| \) continuous at \( x=0 \)?
options: Yes, since the product of two functions continuous at \( x=0 \) is continuous at \( x=0 \), and \( h(0)=0 \)
No, since \( |x| \) is not differentiable at \( x=0 \), so any product involving it is discontinuous there
Cannot be determined without checking \( Lf'(0) \) and \( Rf'(0) \)
No, since \( x^{2}|x| \) is undefined at \( x=0 \)
questions.explanation:
\( f(x)=x^{2} \) is a polynomial, so it is continuous everywhere, including at \( x=0 \).

\( g(x)=|x| \) is also continuous at \( x=0 \), since \( \lim_{x\to0^{-}}|x|=\lim_{x\to0^{+}}|x|=|0|=0 \).

By the algebra of continuous functions, the product \( h=f\cdot g \) is continuous at \( x=0 \), and \( h(0)=0^{2}\cdot|0|=0 \) matches the limit.
questions.hint: Continuity of a product only needs continuity of each factor, not differentiability.
distractor_logic: Differentiability failing at a point does not affect continuity of that function, and continuity of the product only depends on continuity, not differentiability, of the factors
Continuity of a product only requires continuity of the two factors; checking one-sided derivatives is unnecessary and irrelevant here
\( x^2|x| \) is perfectly defined at \( x=0 \), where it equals \( 0 \)

questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\begin{cases}5,& x<1\\ 2x+3,& x\geq1\end{cases} \). Check the continuity of \( f \) at \( x=1 \).
options: Discontinuous at \( x=1 \), since \( \lim_{x\to1^{+}}f(x)=3 \) instead of \( 5 \)
Discontinuous at \( x=1 \), since a constant piece cannot match a linear piece
Continuous, but only in the sense that both pieces are individually continuous, not that \( f \) is continuous at \( x=1 \) itself
questions.explanation:
Compute the left-hand limit using the constant piece: \( \lim_{x\to1^{-}}5=5 \).

Compute the right-hand limit using the second piece: \( \lim_{x\to1^{+}}(2x+3)=2(1)+3=5 \).

Since \( x=1 \) falls in the second piece, \( f(1)=2(1)+3=5 \).

All three values equal \( 5 \), so \( f \) is continuous at \( x=1 \).
questions.hint: A constant function has the same limit from both sides — just check it against the other piece's limit.
distractor_logic: This uses \( 2(1)+3=3 \), an arithmetic slip; the correct value is \( 5 \)
A constant piece can absolutely match a linear piece at a single join point if the values happen to agree there, as they do here

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3},& x\neq3\\ 5,& x=3\end{cases} \). Is \( f \) continuous at \( x=3 \)?
options: Yes, since rational functions are always continuous
No, since the limit does not exist at \( x=3 \)
questions.explanation:
For \( x\neq3 \), factor: \( \dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}=\dfrac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}=x+3 \).

So \( \lim_{x\to3}f(x)=\lim_{x\to3}(x+3)=6 \).

But \( f(3)=5 \) as given, which does not equal \( 6 \).

Since the limit and the function value disagree, \( f \) is not continuous at \( x=3 \) (a removable discontinuity).
questions.hint: Compute the limit by factoring first, then compare it to the stated value of \( f(3) \).
distractor_logic: This reports the wrong limit value; factoring \( x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3) \) and cancelling gives \( \lim_{x\to3}(x+3)=6 \), not \( 5 \)
Rational functions are continuous only on their domain (where the denominator is nonzero); at \( x=3 \) the original expression is undefined, so continuity there must be checked directly, not assumed
The limit does exist and is finite (equal to \( 6 \)) once the removable factor is cancelled; it is only \( f(3) \) that fails to match it

For continuity at \( x=0 \), \( k=f(0) \) must equal this limit.

So \( k=0 \).

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: A three-piece function is defined as \( f(x)=\begin{cases}ax+1,& x<1\\ 3,& x=1\\ bx^{2}+2,& x>1\end{cases} \). Find the values of \( a \) and \( b \) so that \( f \) is continuous at \( x=1 \).
options: No such \( a \) and \( b \) exist, since a three-piece function can never be made continuous at an interior join point
questions.explanation:
For continuity at \( x=1 \), the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and \( f(1)=3 \) must all agree.

Left-hand limit: \( \lim_{x\to1^{-}}(ax+1)=a+1 \). Setting this equal to \( 3 \) gives \( a=2 \).

Right-hand limit: \( \lim_{x\to1^{+}}(bx^{2}+2)=b+2 \). Setting this equal to \( 3 \) gives \( b=1 \).

So \( a=2 \) and \( b=1 \) make \( f \) continuous at \( x=1 \).
questions.hint: Set the left-hand limit equal to \( f(1) \) to solve for \( a \), and the right-hand limit equal to \( f(1) \) to solve for \( b \) — two separate equations.
distractor_logic: This swaps the roles of \( a \) and \( b \): the left piece needs \( a(1)+1=3 \), giving \( a=2 \), and the right piece needs \( b(1)^2+2=3 \), giving \( b=1 \)
This wrongly sets each unknown equal to \( f(1)=3 \) directly, without actually solving \( a(1)+1=3 \) and \( b(1)^2+2=3 \) for \( a \) and \( b \)
A three-piece function can absolutely be made continuous at a join point by matching both one-sided limits to the middle value, exactly as done here

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x},& x\neq0\\ k,& x=0\end{cases} \). Find \( k \) so that \( f \) is continuous at \( x=0 \).
options: \( k \) does not exist, since direct substitution gives \( \frac{0}{0} \)
questions.explanation:
Rationalise the numerator by multiplying by \( \dfrac{\sqrt{x+4}+2}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} \): \( \dfrac{(\sqrt{x+4}-2)(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}=\dfrac{x+4-4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}=\dfrac{x}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} \).

So \( \lim_{x\to0}f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4}+2}=\dfrac{1}{2+2}=\dfrac{1}{4} \).

For continuity, \( k=f(0) \) must equal this limit, so \( k=\dfrac{1}{4} \).
questions.hint: Rationalise the numerator (multiply by its conjugate) before taking the limit.
distractor_logic: This treats the \( \frac{0}{0} \) form at \( x=0 \) as evaluating to \( 0 \) by naive direct substitution, instead of rationalising first
This mistakes the constant \( 2 \) appearing inside the numerator (from \( \sqrt{x+4}-2 \)) for the value of the limit itself
The \( 0/0 \) form only appears under direct substitution; rationalising the numerator removes the common factor and reveals a finite limit

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\dfrac{x^{2}-x-6}{x^{2}-9} \). At which point does \( f \) have a removable discontinuity, and what value would extend \( f \) continuously there?
options: Removable discontinuity at \( x=-3 \); the extended value is \( \dfrac{5}{6} \)
Removable discontinuity at \( x=3 \); the extended value is \( 0 \)
Removable discontinuity at \( x=3 \); the extended value is \( \dfrac{5}{6} \)
There is no removable discontinuity, since \( x^{2}-9 \) factors with no common terms
questions.explanation:
Factor both numerator and denominator: \( x^{2}-x-6=(x-3)(x+2) \) and \( x^{2}-9=(x-3)(x+3) \).

The common factor \( (x-3) \) cancels for \( x\neq3 \), giving \( f(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{x+3} \), which is defined and continuous at \( x=3 \).

So the discontinuity at \( x=3 \) is removable, with limiting value \( \dfrac{3+2}{3+3}=\dfrac{5}{6} \).

At \( x=-3 \), the factor \( (x+3) \) remains in the denominator with no cancelling numerator factor, so that discontinuity is not removable.
questions.hint: Factor numerator and denominator fully; a discontinuity is removable only where a factor cancels.
distractor_logic: The common factor that cancels is \( (x-3) \), which comes from the zero of the denominator at \( x=3 \), not \( x=-3 \); the point \( x=-3 \) remains a genuine (non-removable) discontinuity where the numerator does not vanish
This comes from directly (and invalidly) substituting \( x=3 \) into the unfactored \( \frac{0}{0} \) form and reading it as \( 0 \), rather than cancelling the common factor first
\( x^2-x-6 \) and \( x^2-9 \) do in fact share the common factor \( (x-3) \), which is exactly what creates the removable discontinuity

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Let \( f(x)=\begin{cases}x+1,& x<2\\ 3,& 2\leq x<4\\ 2x-5,& x\geq4\end{cases} \). Check the continuity of \( f \) at \( x=2 \) and at \( x=4 \).
options: Discontinuous at both \( x=2 \) and \( x=4 \)
Continuous at \( x=4 \) but discontinuous at \( x=2 \), since the left piece is linear and the middle piece is constant
Continuous at \( x=2 \) but discontinuous at \( x=4 \), since \( \lim_{x\to4^{-}}f(x)=3 \) while \( f(4)=3 \) should be treated as not matching
Continuous at both \( x=2 \) and \( x=4 \), since LHL, RHL, and the function value all equal \( 3 \) at each join point
questions.explanation:
At \( x=2 \): \( \lim_{x\to2^{-}}(x+1)=2+1=3 \); \( \lim_{x\to2^{+}}3=3 \); \( f(2)=3 \) (from the middle piece, since \( 2\leq x<4 \)). All three agree, so \( f \) is continuous at \( x=2 \).

At \( x=4 \): \( \lim_{x\to4^{-}}3=3 \); \( \lim_{x\to4^{+}}(2x-5)=2(4)-5=3 \); \( f(4)=2(4)-5=3 \) (from the third piece, since \( x\geq4 \)). All three agree, so \( f \) is also continuous at \( x=4 \).

Hence \( f \) is continuous at both join points.
questions.hint: Check LHL, RHL, and the function value separately at each of the two join points; use the piece that actually applies to the join point itself.
distractor_logic: Direct computation shows all three quantities (LHL, RHL, and the function value) agree at each of these two points, so \( f \) is in fact continuous at both
A linear piece meeting a constant piece is not automatically discontinuous — here \( \lim_{x\to2^{-}}(x+1)=3 \) exactly matches the constant piece's value of \( 3 \), so the join is continuous
\( f(4)=2(4)-5=3 \) genuinely equals the left-hand limit of \( 3 \); a correctly computed equal value should not be dismissed as not matching

questions.topic: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
questions.question: Consider \( f \) redefined piecewise near \( x=2 \) as \( f(x)=\begin{cases}x-1,& x<2\\ 0,& x=2\\ x-2,& x>2\end{cases} \). Explain why \( f \) is discontinuous at \( x=2 \), identifying which of the two failure modes of continuity occurs.
options: The one-sided limits themselves disagree: \( \lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=1 \) but \( \lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)=0 \), so \( \lim_{x\to2}f(x) \) does not exist at all — a more fundamental failure than a limit that exists but merely fails to equal \( f(2) \)
The limit exists and equals \( 0 \), and \( f(2)=0 \) too, so \( f \) is actually continuous
The limit exists and equals \( 1 \), but \( f(2)=0 \) does not match it — a removable discontinuity
\( f \) is discontinuous only because \( f(2) \) is undefined
questions.explanation:
Compute the left-hand limit: \( \lim_{x\to2^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^{-}}(x-1)=2-1=1 \).

Compute the right-hand limit: \( \lim_{x\to2^{+}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^{+}}(x-2)=2-2=0 \).

Since \( 1\neq0 \), the left-hand and right-hand limits disagree, so \( \lim_{x\to2}f(x) \) does not exist at all.

This is different from a removable discontinuity, where the two-sided limit would exist but simply fail to match \( f(2) \); here the limit itself never forms, which is the more fundamental of the two ways continuity can fail.
questions.hint: Compute both one-sided limits first — if they disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist at all, which is a different failure than a limit that exists but misses \( f(a) \).
distractor_logic: Direct computation of the left-hand limit gives \( \lim_{x\to2^{-}}(x-1)=1 \), which does not equal the right-hand limit of \( 0 \); the two one-sided limits genuinely disagree, so \( f \) is not continuous

The right-hand limit is \( \lim_{x\to2^{+}}(x-2)=0 \), not \( 1 \); since the two one-sided limits themselves disagree (\( 1\neq0 \)), the two-sided limit fails to exist in the first place, a different and more fundamental failure than a removable discontinuity
\( f(2) \) is explicitly defined as \( 0 \) by the middle piece; the actual problem is that the one-sided limits disagree, not that the function value is missing

questions.question: Explain why \( y=[f(x)]^{g(x)} \), with both \( f(x) \) and \( g(x) \) non-constant, cannot be differentiated using the power rule alone or the exponential rule alone.
options: The power rule and exponential rule both still apply here, and logarithmic differentiation is only needed as an optional shortcut for convenience, not out of necessity

questions.explanation:
The power rule requires the exponent to be a fixed constant, and the exponential rule requires the base to be a fixed constant.

In \( y=[f(x)]^{g(x)} \), both quantities vary with \( x \), so neither hypothesis is met, and neither rule can be applied directly.

Logarithmic differentiation resolves this by taking \( \ln \) of both sides, turning the troublesome exponentiation into the product \( g(x)\ln f(x) \) via \( \ln y=g(x)\ln f(x) \), which can then be differentiated using the ordinary product rule and chain rule, before multiplying back by \( y \) to isolate \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.hint: Ask which rule assumes what is fixed (exponent for power rule, base for exponential rule) — here neither assumption holds.
distractor_logic: Neither rule's underlying assumption (fixed exponent for the power rule, fixed base for the exponential rule) is actually satisfied when both base and exponent vary, so applying either one directly gives an incorrect derivative — logarithmic differentiation is necessary here, not merely a convenient alternative

questions.question: If \( x=f(t) \) and \( y=g(t) \), what is the formula for \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) in terms of derivatives with respect to \( t \)?
questions.explanation: When \( x \) and \( y \) are both given in terms of a third variable \( t \), the parametric derivative formula is \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \), valid provided \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}\neq0 \).
questions.hint: Divide the rate of change of \( y \) with respect to \( t \) by the rate of change of \( x \) with respect to \( t \).
distractor_logic: This inverts the correct ratio; the numerator should be \( dy/dt \) and the denominator \( dx/dt \), not the other way around
This uses only \( dy/dt \) alone and forgets to divide by \( dx/dt \), which is required whenever \( x \) also depends on the parameter \( t \)
This multiplies the two parametric derivatives together instead of dividing one by the other

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: What condition must hold for the parametric derivative formula \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \) to be valid?
options: No condition is needed; the formula always holds
questions.explanation:
Since the formula is a quotient \( \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \), the denominator must not vanish.

The formula \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \) is valid provided \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}\neq0 \).
questions.hint: It's a fraction — the bottom quantity can't be zero.
distractor_logic: It is the denominator \( dx/dt \), not the numerator \( dy/dt \), whose non-vanishing matters here, since division by zero must be avoided
A ratio with both quantities equal to zero gives an indeterminate \( \frac{0}{0} \) form, not a valid derivative; the actual requirement is simply that the denominator alone be nonzero
Division by zero is undefined, so the formula requires \( dx/dt\neq0 \); ignoring this condition entirely is incorrect

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: For \( x=f(t) \), \( y=g(t) \), what is the correct formula for the second derivative \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \)?
questions.explanation:
The correct method never differentiates \( x \) and \( y \) separately a second time and divides.

Instead: \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}} \) — differentiate \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) with respect to \( t \), then divide by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \) again.
questions.hint: Treat \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) itself as the new function to differentiate with respect to \( t \), then divide by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) once more — never touch \( x \) and \( y \)'s second \( t \)-derivatives directly.
distractor_logic: This is the central trap of this topic: taking the second \( t \)-derivatives of \( y \) and \( x \) separately and dividing them does NOT give the correct second derivative with respect to \( x \)

This stops one step early; after differentiating \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) with respect to \( t \), the result must still be divided by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) to convert it into a derivative with respect to \( x \)

Squaring the first-derivative formula is not how a second derivative is computed; the correct method differentiates \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) itself with respect to \( t \), then divides by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \)

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: Is it true that \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{d^{2}y/dt^{2}}{d^{2}x/dt^{2}} \) for parametric equations \( x=f(t) \), \( y=g(t) \)?
options: Yes — this is exactly the correct formula for the parametric second derivative
No — this shortcut is incorrect in general; the genuine second derivative requires differentiating \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) with respect to \( t \) first, then dividing by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \)
Yes, but only when \( x=t \) exactly
The two formulas are always equal by the chain rule
questions.explanation:
This equality is false in general and is the central trap of this topic.

The correct formula is \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt} \): differentiate \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) with respect to \( t \), then divide by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \) again — never simply divide the two separate second \( t \)-derivatives.
questions.hint: This is the chapter's central trap — always use the two-step method, never the direct ratio of second \( t \)-derivatives.
distractor_logic: This is the central trap of the topic; simply taking the ratio of the two separate second \( t \)-derivatives does not correctly account for how \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) itself changes with \( t \), and gives a genuinely different (wrong) answer in general

Even in that special case the two formulas may happen to coincide for trivial reasons, but this does not make the shortcut formula correct as a general method — the proper two-step formula should still be used
The chain rule does not make these two expressions equal in general; a direct comparison on a specific example (such as \( x=t^2 \), \( y=t^3 \)) shows they give different numerical values

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: In the parametric equations \( x=f(t) \), \( y=g(t) \), what are \( \dfrac{dy}{dt} \) and \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \)?
options: Partial derivatives of \( y \) and \( x \) with respect to each other
The same quantity as \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) and \( \dfrac{dx}{dy} \), just written differently
Ordinary derivatives of \( y \) and \( x \) taken separately with respect to the single variable \( t \)
Constants, since \( t \) is treated as a fixed parameter throughout
questions.explanation: Since \( x \) and \( y \) are each given explicitly as functions of the single variable \( t \), \( \dfrac{dy}{dt} \) and \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \) are ordinary (single-variable) derivatives, computed just like any other derivative with respect to \( t \).
questions.hint: Both \( x \) and \( y \) are ordinary single-variable functions — just of \( t \) instead of each other.
distractor_logic: Neither \( x \) nor \( y \) is being differentiated with respect to the other directly; both are separately differentiated with respect to the third variable \( t \), so no partial derivatives are involved

\( \frac{dy}{dt} \) and \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) are derivatives with respect to the parameter \( t \), which is a different variable from \( x \) or \( y \) themselves; \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) is instead built from these two quantities by dividing one by the other
\( t \) is the variable being differentiated with respect to, not a fixed constant; \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) and \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) are themselves functions of \( t \) in general, not constants

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: What is the standard term for a pair of equations \( x=f(t) \), \( y=g(t) \) that describe a curve through a third variable \( t \)?
options: Implicit equations, with \( t \) called the implicit variable
Piecewise equations, with \( t \) called the join variable
Inverse equations, with \( t \) called the inverse variable
Parametric equations, with \( t \) called the parameter
questions.explanation: When both coordinates of a curve are given as separate functions of a third variable, that variable is called the parameter, and the equations are called parametric equations: \( x=f(t) \), \( y=g(t) \).
questions.hint: Think of \( t \) as tracing out the curve — hence "parametric."
distractor_logic: An implicit equation relates \( x \) and \( y \) directly in a single equation like \( F(x,y)=0 \), without introducing any third variable; this is a different situation from expressing both \( x \) and \( y \) via a separate variable \( t \)
A piecewise definition switches between different formulas over different intervals of a single variable; it does not involve expressing \( x \) and \( y \) both through a separate third variable
Inverse functions swap the roles of the input and output of a single function; that is unrelated to expressing \( x \) and \( y \) both in terms of a separate parameter \( t \)

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: To find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) when \( x=f(t) \) and \( y=g(t) \) are both given, is it necessary to first eliminate \( t \) and rewrite \( y \) explicitly as a function of \( x \)?
options: No — \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) can be found directly as the ratio \( \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \), without ever eliminating \( t \)
Yes — eliminating \( t \) first is always required before differentiating
Yes, but only for trigonometric parametric equations
It depends on whether \( x=f(t) \) is a one-to-one function
questions.explanation:
The entire point of the parametric derivative formula is to avoid having to eliminate the parameter.

\( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \) can be computed directly from the two separate ordinary derivatives \( \dfrac{dy}{dt} \) and \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \), without ever solving for \( t \) in terms of \( x \).
questions.hint: The formula is built precisely so that elimination of the parameter is never required.
distractor_logic: Eliminating the parameter is unnecessary and often impossible or impractical; the parametric derivative formula \( \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \) gives \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) directly using the two separate \( t \)-derivatives
There is no such restriction; the direct ratio formula \( \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \) works for any parametric pair meeting the stated condition, not just trigonometric ones

While eliminating \( t \) would technically require \( f \) to be invertible, the parametric derivative formula sidesteps this issue entirely by working directly with the two separate \( t \)-derivatives, regardless of whether \( f \) is one-to-one

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: In the correct formula \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt} \), with respect to which variable must \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) be differentiated in the numerator?
options: With respect to \( x \) directly, since \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \) is ultimately a derivative with respect to \( x \)
With respect to \( t \), not directly with respect to \( x \)
With respect to \( y \), since the expression being differentiated is \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \)
It does not matter which variable is used, since the final result is the same either way
questions.explanation: Since \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) is itself expressed in terms of the parameter \( t \) (after computing it as \( \dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \)), the correct next step is to differentiate this expression with respect to \( t \), and only then divide by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \) to obtain \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \).
questions.hint: \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) is a function of \( t \) at this stage of the calculation — differentiate it as such.
distractor_logic: Although the final second derivative is with respect to \( x \), the intermediate step differentiates \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) with respect to the parameter \( t \) (since \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) is itself expressed in terms of \( t \)); only after that does dividing by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) convert the result into a derivative with respect to \( x \)

\( \frac{dy}{dx} \) is a function of the parameter \( t \) (once \( x \) and \( y \) are both expressed via \( t \)), not a function of \( y \) itself, so differentiating with respect to \( y \) does not apply here

The variable of differentiation matters a great deal; differentiating with respect to the wrong variable does not produce \( \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) \), and the subsequent division by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) would then be meaningless

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=t^{2} \) and \( y=t^{3} \), find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=2t \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=3t^{2} \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{3t^{2}}{2t}=\dfrac{3t}{2} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate \( x \) and \( y \) separately with respect to \( t \), then divide and simplify.
distractor_logic: This reports \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) alone and forgets to divide by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=2t \)
This inverts the correct ratio, placing \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) in the numerator and \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) in the denominator instead of the other way around
This divides the coefficients but drops a power of \( t \) incorrectly rather than correctly simplifying \( \frac{3t^2}{2t} \) to \( \frac{3t}{2} \)

questions.question: If \( x=3t \) and \( y=t^{2}+1 \), find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=3 \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=2t \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{2t}{3} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate \( x \) and \( y \) separately with respect to \( t \), then divide.
distractor_logic: This reports \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) alone and forgets to divide by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=3 \)
This inverts the correct ratio, placing \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) in the numerator and \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) in the denominator instead of the other way around

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=\cos t \) and \( y=\sin t \), find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\sin t \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=\cos t \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{\cos t}{-\sin t}=-\cot t \).
questions.hint: Don't forget the negative sign in \( \frac{d}{dt}(\cos t)=-\sin t \) when forming the ratio.
distractor_logic: The sign is wrong; since \( \frac{dx}{dt}=-\sin t \) is negative, dividing \( \cos t \) by \( -\sin t \) introduces a minus sign, giving \( -\cot t \), not \( \cot t \)

This inverts the correct ratio; dividing \( \frac{dy}{dt}=\cos t \) by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=-\sin t \) gives \( -\cot t \), not \( \tan t \), which would instead come from dividing \( \sin t \) by \( \cos t \)
This reports \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) alone rather than the actual ratio \( \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \)

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=t+1 \) and \( y=t^{2}-2t \), find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=1 \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=2t-2 \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{2t-2}{1}=2t-2 \).
questions.hint: Since \( \frac{dx}{dt}=1 \) here, \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) equals \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) directly.
distractor_logic: This wrongly divides by an extra factor of \( 2 \); the correct \( \frac{dx}{dt}=1 \), so no division beyond the identity ratio is needed
This drops the constant term \( -2 \) that comes from differentiating \( -2t \) inside \( \frac{dy}{dt}=2t-2 \)

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=e^{t} \) and \( y=e^{2t} \), find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=e^{t} \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=2e^{2t} \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{2e^{2t}}{e^{t}}=2e^{t} \).
questions.hint: Simplify the exponentials using \( \frac{e^{2t}}{e^{t}}=e^{t} \).
distractor_logic: This reports \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) alone and forgets to divide by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=e^{t} \)
This reports \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) alone rather than the actual ratio \( \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \)

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=at^{2} \) and \( y=2at \), where \( a \) is a nonzero constant, find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=2at \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=2a \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{2a}{2at}=\dfrac{1}{t} \).
questions.hint: The constant \( 2a \) cancels between numerator and denominator, leaving only a \( t \) in the denominator.

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=t^{3} \) and \( y=t^{2} \), find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=3t^{2} \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=2t \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{2t}{3t^{2}}=\dfrac{2}{3t} \).
questions.hint: Cancel a common factor of \( t \) from numerator and denominator carefully.
distractor_logic: This inverts the correct ratio; dividing \( \frac{dy}{dt}=2t \) by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=3t^2 \) gives \( \frac{2}{3t} \), not its reciprocal

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=1-t^{2} \) and \( y=2t \), find \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \).
questions.explanation:
Compute the two separate ordinary derivatives: \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=-2t \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=2 \).

By the parametric formula, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{2}{-2t}=-\dfrac{1}{t} \).
questions.hint: Don't drop the negative sign that comes from differentiating \( 1-t^2 \).
distractor_logic: The sign is wrong; since \( \frac{dx}{dt}=-2t \) is negative, dividing \( \frac{dy}{dt}=2 \) by it introduces a minus sign

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=t^{2} \) and \( y=t^{3} \), find \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \), using the correct two-step formula.
questions.explanation:
First, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{3t^{2}}{2t}=\dfrac{3t}{2} \).

Differentiate this with respect to \( t \): \( \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{3t}{2}\right)=\dfrac{3}{2} \).

Divide by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=2t \): \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{3/2}{2t}=\dfrac{3}{4t} \).
questions.hint: First find \( \frac{dy}{dx} \), then differentiate that result with respect to \( t \), then divide by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \) — three separate steps.
distractor_logic: This uses the trap shortcut \( \frac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}=\frac{6t}{2}=3t \) instead of the correct two-step method, which gives a genuinely different value
This computes \( \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)=\frac{3}{2} \) correctly as the numerator, but then forgets the required final division by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=2t \)
This inverts the correct ratio between the numerator \( \frac{3}{2} \) and the denominator \( 2t \)

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=at^{2} \) and \( y=2at \), where \( a \) is a nonzero constant, find \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \).
questions.explanation:
First, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{2a}{2at}=\dfrac{1}{t} \).

Differentiate this with respect to \( t \): \( \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{1}{t}\right)=-\dfrac{1}{t^{2}} \).

Divide by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=2at \): \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{-1/t^{2}}{2at}=-\dfrac{1}{2at^{3}} \).
questions.hint: Differentiate \( \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{t} \) with respect to \( t \) first (giving \( -\frac{1}{t^2} \)), then divide by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \).
distractor_logic: This wrongly uses the trap shortcut \( \frac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}=\frac{0}{2a}=0 \) (since \( y=2at \) is linear in \( t \)); but this shortcut is invalid, and the correct two-step method gives a nonzero result
This drops the negative sign that arises when differentiating \( \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{t} \) with respect to \( t \), which gives \( -\frac{1}{t^2} \), not \( \frac{1}{t^2} \)

This divides by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=2at \) correctly in form but uses \( \frac{1}{t} \) as the numerator instead of the actual result of differentiating \( \frac{dy}{dx} \), which is \( -\frac{1}{t^2} \)

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=\cos t \) and \( y=\sin t \), find \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \).
questions.explanation:
First, \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\dfrac{\cos t}{-\sin t}=-\cot t \).

Differentiate this with respect to \( t \): \( \dfrac{d}{dt}(-\cot t)=\text{cosec}^{2}t \).

Divide by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\sin t \): \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{\text{cosec}^{2}t}{-\sin t}=-\text{cosec}^{2}t\cdot\text{cosec}\,t=-\text{cosec}^{3}t \).
questions.hint: Remember \( \frac{d}{dt}(-\cot t)=\text{cosec}^2t \), and that dividing by \( -\sin t \) is the same as multiplying by \( -\text{cosec}\,t \).
distractor_logic: This computes \( \frac{d}{dt}(-\cot t)=\csc^2t \) correctly for the numerator step, but then simplifies the final division by \( \frac{dx}{dt}=-\sin t \) incorrectly, missing an extra power of \( \csc t \)
The overall sign is wrong; dividing \( \csc^2t \) by the negative quantity \( -\sin t \) must produce a negative result

This uses the trap shortcut \( \frac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2}=\frac{-\sin t}{-\cos t} \) evaluated incorrectly, rather than the valid two-step method; the trap shortcut itself is not a legitimate way to find this second derivative

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: For \( x=t^{2} \), \( y=t^{3} \), compute both \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \) using the correct two-step formula and the value given by the trap shortcut \( \dfrac{d^{2}y/dt^{2}}{d^{2}x/dt^{2}} \), at \( t=1 \). Do they agree?
options: No — the correct two-step formula gives \( \dfrac{3}{4} \) at \( t=1 \), while the trap shortcut gives \( 3 \) at \( t=1 \); the two disagree, confirming the shortcut is invalid
They cannot be compared, since parametric second derivatives have no numerical value at a specific point
questions.explanation:
Correct method: \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3t}{2} \), so \( \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{3t}{2}\right)=\dfrac{3}{2} \), and \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{3/2}{2t}=\dfrac{3}{4t} \). At \( t=1 \), this gives \( \dfrac{3}{4} \).

Trap shortcut: \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}}=6t \) and \( \dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}=2 \), so the (invalid) shortcut ratio is \( \dfrac{6t}{2}=3t \). At \( t=1 \), this gives \( 3 \).

Since \( \dfrac{3}{4}\neq3 \), the two methods genuinely disagree, confirming numerically why the shortcut must never be used.
questions.hint: Compute both quantities separately at \( t=1 \) and compare the actual numbers — this is the cleanest way to see why the shortcut fails.
distractor_logic: The correct two-step formula, \( \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{3}{4t} \), evaluates to \( \frac{3}{4} \) at \( t=1 \), not \( 3 \); only the invalid trap shortcut gives \( 3 \)

A parametric second derivative is a genuine function of \( t \) (or, indirectly, of \( x \)) and can absolutely be evaluated at a specific value of \( t \), exactly like any other derivative

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=t-\sin t \) and \( y=1-\cos t \) (a cycloid), find \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \).
questions.explanation:
First, \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=1-\cos t \) and \( \dfrac{dy}{dt}=\sin t \), so \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\sin t}{1-\cos t} \).

Differentiate this with respect to \( t \) using the quotient rule: \( \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{\sin t}{1-\cos t}\right)=\dfrac{\cos t(1-\cos t)-\sin t(\sin t)}{(1-\cos t)^{2}}=\dfrac{\cos t-\cos^{2}t-\sin^{2}t}{(1-\cos t)^{2}}=\dfrac{\cos t-1}{(1-\cos t)^{2}}=\dfrac{-1}{1-\cos t} \).

Divide by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=1-\cos t \): \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{-1/(1-\cos t)}{1-\cos t}=-\dfrac{1}{(1-\cos t)^{2}} \).
questions.hint: Use the quotient rule to differentiate \( \frac{\sin t}{1-\cos t} \) with respect to \( t \); the identity \( \cos^2t+\sin^2t=1 \) simplifies the numerator nicely.
distractor_logic: This leaves the numerator as \( \sin t \) instead of correctly carrying out the quotient-rule differentiation of \( \dfrac{\sin t}{1-\cos t} \) with respect to \( t \), then dividing again by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \)

This uses the trap shortcut \( \frac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2} \) rather than the valid two-step method of differentiating \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) with respect to \( t \) and then dividing by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \)
This is missing the required squaring of \( (1-\cos t) \) in the denominator that arises from correctly carrying out the full two-step differentiation

questions.topic: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
questions.question: If \( x=t^{3}+1 \) and \( y=t^{2}-t \), find \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \).

First derivative: for \( x\leq1 \), \( f'(x)=3x^{2} \), giving \( Lf'(1)=3 \); for \( x>1 \), \( f'(x)=6x-3 \), giving \( Rf'(1)=6(1)-3=3 \). They match, so \( f \) is differentiable at \( x=1 \).

Second derivative: for \( x\leq1 \), \( f''(x)=6x \), giving \( 6 \) at \( x=1 \); for \( x>1 \), \( f''(x)=6 \) (constant). They match too — this piecewise function has been constructed so that even its second derivative is continuous across the join, a stronger condition than differentiability alone requires.
questions.hint: Check value, first derivative, and second derivative separately at the join point — each is its own independent condition.
distractor_logic: Despite being different-looking expressions, both pieces were specifically constructed to agree in value, first derivative, AND second derivative at \( x=1 \); direct computation confirms \( f''(1)=6 \) from both the cubic piece and the quadratic piece
Correctly differentiating the second piece gives \( f'(x)=6x-3 \), so \( Rf'(1)=6(1)-3=3 \), matching \( Lf'(1)=3(1)^2=3 \) exactly — the two one-sided derivatives actually agree

Genuinely matching values from both sides at the join point, however the match arose, is exactly what continuity requires; there is no sense in which a correctly computed equal value should be dismissed as an insufficient coincidence

topics.name: Continuity: Definition and Algebra of Continuous Functions
topics.summary: A function \( f \) is continuous at \( x=a \) when \( \lim_{x\to a^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^{+}}f(x)=f(a) \) — the left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value must all agree. Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational functions are continuous wherever their denominator is nonzero. Sums, differences, and products of continuous functions stay continuous with no extra condition, but a quotient needs the denominator to be nonzero at that point. For piecewise functions built from polynomials and trigonometric pieces, checking continuity at a join point means computing all three quantities separately and comparing them — never skipping straight to a conclusion. Evaluating these limits sometimes requires factoring and cancelling a common factor (revealing a removable discontinuity), or using the standard trigonometric limits \( \lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1 \) and \( \lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x}=0 \), never anything beyond direct substitution, factoring, or these two limits.
key_formulas: \( f \) continuous at \( x=a \) \( \iff \) \( \lim_{x\to a^{-}}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^{+}}f(x)=f(a) \)
Sum/difference/product of continuous functions is continuous; quotient is continuous where the denominator is nonzero
topics.worked_example: Let \( f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^{2}-4}{x-2},& x\neq2\\ k,& x=2\end{cases} \). For \( x\neq2 \), factor: \( \dfrac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2 \), so \( \lim_{x\to2}f(x)=4 \). For continuity, \( f(2)=k \) must equal this limit, so \( k=4 \).
common_mistakes: Checking only one of LHL/RHL/\( f(a) \) instead of confirming all three agree
Substituting directly into a \( 0/0 \) form instead of factoring and cancelling first
Assuming a rational function is continuous everywhere without excluding the zeros of its denominator

topics.name: Differentiability, the Chain Rule, and Implicit Differentiation
topics.summary: A function is differentiable at \( x=a \) when \( Lf'(a)=\lim_{h\to0^{-}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \) and \( Rf'(a)=\lim_{h\to0^{+}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \) are equal and finite. Differentiability always implies continuity, but continuity never guarantees differentiability — \( f(x)=|x| \) is the standard example, continuous but not differentiable at \( x=0 \) since its one-sided derivatives disagree. The chain rule differentiates a composite function as \( f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x) \); the product rule gives \( u'v+uv' \); the quotient rule gives \( \frac{u'v-uv'}{v^{2}} \). Implicit differentiation applies these same rules to relations that mix \( x \) and \( y \) together, remembering to attach \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) every time a \( y \)-term is differentiated, then solving algebraically for \( \frac{dy}{dx} \).
key_formulas: \( f \) differentiable at \( x=a \) \( \iff \) \( Lf'(a)=Rf'(a) \), both finite
topics.worked_example: For \( x^{2}+y^{2}=25 \), differentiate both sides: \( 2x+2y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0 \). Isolating gives \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{x}{y} \) — note the \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) attached to the \( y^2 \) term via the chain rule.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inner function when applying the chain rule
Assuming continuity at a point automatically means the function is also differentiable there
Differentiating a \( y \)-term implicitly without attaching \( \frac{dy}{dx} \)

topics.name: Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric, Exponential and Logarithmic Functions; Logarithmic Differentiation
topics.summary: Standard derivative formulas: \( \frac{d}{dx}(\sin^{-1}x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}} \), \( \frac{d}{dx}(\cos^{-1}x)=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}} \), \( \frac{d}{dx}(\tan^{-1}x)=\frac{1}{1+x^{2}} \), \( \frac{d}{dx}(\cot^{-1}x)=\frac{-1}{1+x^{2}} \), with similar formulas for \( \sec^{-1}x \) and \( \text{cosec}^{-1}x \). For exponentials, \( \frac{d}{dx}(e^{x})=e^{x} \) and \( \frac{d}{dx}(a^{x})=a^{x}\ln a \); for logarithms, \( \frac{d}{dx}(\ln x)=\frac{1}{x} \) and \( \frac{d}{dx}(\log_{a}x)=\frac{1}{x\ln a} \). The central distinction of this topic is recognising which of three cases applies: constant base with variable exponent (power rule), constant exponent with variable base (exponential rule), or both varying — which requires logarithmic differentiation. For \( y=[f(x)]^{g(x)} \), take \( \ln \) of both sides to get \( \ln y=g(x)\ln f(x) \), differentiate, then multiply back by \( y \) to isolate \( \frac{dy}{dx} \).
topics.worked_example: For \( y=x^{x} \), take \( \ln \) of both sides: \( \ln y=x\ln x \). Differentiate: \( \dfrac{1}{y}\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\ln x+1 \). Multiply back by \( y=x^{x} \): \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=x^{x}(\ln x+1) \).
common_mistakes: Applying the plain power rule or exponential rule to \( [f(x)]^{g(x)} \) instead of using logarithmic differentiation
Forgetting to multiply the final result back by \( y \) after logarithmic differentiation
Confusing the derivative of an inverse trig function with the derivative of the trig function itself

topics.name: Parametric Differentiation and Second Order Derivatives
topics.summary: When \( x=f(t) \) and \( y=g(t) \) are both given in terms of a parameter \( t \), \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} \), provided \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}\neq0 \) — computed directly, with no need to eliminate \( t \). The central trap of this topic is the second derivative: \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \) is never \( \dfrac{d^{2}y/dt^{2}}{d^{2}x/dt^{2}} \). The correct method differentiates \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} \) itself with respect to \( t \), then divides by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt} \) again: \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{dx/dt} \). This topic also covers ordinary second derivatives of ordinary (non-parametric) functions built from polynomials, trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic pieces, requiring the chain, product, or quotient rule applied twice in succession. No derivative in this chapter ever goes beyond the second order.
topics.worked_example: For \( x=t^{2} \), \( y=t^{3} \): \( \dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{3t^{2}}{2t}=\dfrac{3t}{2} \). Then \( \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{3t}{2}\right)=\dfrac{3}{2} \), and dividing by \( \dfrac{dx}{dt}=2t \) gives \( \dfrac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=\dfrac{3}{4t} \) — not the \( 3t \) that the trap shortcut would incorrectly give.
common_mistakes: Computing the parametric second derivative as \( \frac{d^2y/dt^2}{d^2x/dt^2} \) instead of the correct two-step formula
Computing \( \frac{dy}{dx} \) as \( \frac{dy}{dt} \) alone, forgetting to divide by \( \frac{dx}{dt} \)
Not checking where \( \frac{dx}{dt}=0 \) makes the parametric derivative formula undefined

topics.name: Mean Value Theorems: Rolle's Theorem and Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem
topics.summary: Rolle's Theorem: if \( f \) is continuous on \( [a,b] \), differentiable on \( (a,b) \), and \( f(a)=f(b) \), then some \( c\in(a,b) \) has \( f'(c)=0 \). Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT) drops the equal-endpoints requirement: if \( f \) is continuous on \( [a,b] \) and differentiable on \( (a,b) \), then some \( c\in(a,b) \) has \( f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \). Rolle's Theorem is the special case of LMVT where \( f(a)=f(b) \), making the right-hand side zero — geometrically, LMVT guarantees a tangent parallel to the secant line joining the endpoints, and Rolle's is the case where that secant is horizontal. Applying either theorem always starts by verifying its hypotheses hold — continuity on the closed interval, differentiability on the open interval, and (for Rolle's) equal endpoint values — before solving for \( c \) and checking it genuinely lies inside the open interval, discarding any algebraic solution that lands on an endpoint instead.
key_formulas: Rolle's Theorem: continuous on \( [a,b] \), differentiable on \( (a,b) \), \( f(a)=f(b) \) \( \Rightarrow \) \( f'(c)=0 \) for some \( c\in(a,b) \)
LMVT: continuous on \( [a,b] \), differentiable on \( (a,b) \) \( \Rightarrow \) \( f'(c)=\dfrac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} \) for some \( c\in(a,b) \)
topics.worked_example: For \( f(x)=x^{2}-4x+3 \) on \( [1,3] \): \( f(1)=f(3)=0 \), so Rolle's Theorem applies. Solving \( f'(x)=2x-4=0 \) gives \( x=2 \), which lies in \( (1,3) \), so \( c=2 \).
common_mistakes: Applying Rolle's Theorem without checking \( f(a)=f(b) \), or applying either theorem without verifying continuity and differentiability
Accepting a solution to \( f'(c)=0 \) (or the LMVT equation) that lands exactly on an endpoint, rather than strictly inside the open interval
Assuming matching endpoint values alone are enough for Rolle's Theorem, without also checking differentiability throughout the open interval
